lesson.title: Sliding Without Changing Shape: Translation
lesson.summary: A translation moves every point of a graph the same distance in the same direction, preserving its exact size and shape.
lesson.body:
A translation is a transformation that slides a graph up, down, left, or right without changing its size, shape, or orientation in any way; every point moves the same distance in the same direction, so the translated graph is an exact congruent copy of the original, just relocated. Translations are produced by adding or subtracting constants to a parent function, either outside the function for a vertical slide or inside the function, attached to x, for a horizontal slide.

Vertical translations are the more intuitive of the two: in g(x) = f(x) + k, adding a positive k shifts the whole graph up by k units, and a negative k shifts it down. Horizontal translations work the opposite way from what most people expect: in g(x) = f(x - h), a positive h shifts the graph to the right, and a negative h shifts it left. The reason is that x - h needs a larger x to produce the same output the parent function produced at a smaller input, so the entire graph effectively has to move rightward to reach those same output values, and writing f(x - (-3)) as f(x + 3) is what a leftward shift of 3 actually looks like.

Consider the parent absolute value function f(x) = |x|, whose vertex sits at the origin, transformed into g(x) = |x - 2| + 3. Here h = 2 and k = 3, so the graph should slide 2 units right and 3 units up, moving the vertex from (0, 0) to (2, 3). Confirm this directly: g(2) = |2 - 2| + 3 = |0| + 3 = 0 + 3 = 3, so the point (2, 3) is indeed on the graph, matching the predicted vertex.

Check that the shape is preserved, not just the vertex, by comparing corresponding points. The parent function gives f(1) = |1| = 1. On the translated graph, moving 1 unit right of the new vertex means checking x = 3: g(3) = |3 - 2| + 3 = |1| + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4, which is exactly 3 more than f(1) = 1, consistent with the vertical shift of 3. Similarly, f(-1) = |-1| = 1, and shifting that point 2 right and 3 up should land at (1, 4): g(1) = |1 - 2| + 3 = |-1| + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4, confirming the match.

Translations show up constantly outside of pure graphing, too. If a repair shop's base labor cost is modeled by the parent function f(x) = x, where x is hours worked, and the shop then adds a flat 40 dollar service call fee, the new cost function is g(x) = f(x) + 40 = x + 40, a vertical translation of 40 units. A 3-hour repair costs g(3) = 3 + 40 = 43 dollars, exactly 40 more than the 3 dollars the bare parent function would have predicted, which is the vertical shift showing up directly in a real price.

Because every point moves by the identical amount, h units horizontally and k units vertically, the translated graph is never stretched, squished, or flipped, only relocated, which is what separates a pure translation from the reflections you will study next, where the graph's orientation itself changes.
